A.explanation: This gives only the small negative area from $t = 16\text{ s}$ to $t = 20\text{ s}$, ignoring the large positive area from $0$ to $16\text{ s}$.

B.explanation: Positive area $0$ to $16\text{ s}$ is $24\text{ m}$ and negative area $16$ to $20\text{ s}$ is $-3\text{ m}$, giving $24 - 3 = 21\text{ m}$.

C.explanation: This is the area of the positive triangle only up to $t = 16\text{ s}$, so it forgets to subtract the displacement below the time axis between $16\text{ s}$ and $20\text{ s}$.

D.explanation: This adds the $3\text{ m}$ magnitude below the axis instead of subtracting it, treating distance travelled as displacement.

hints: Notice where the velocity-time graph crosses the $t$-axis at $t = 16\text{ s}$ and what the sign of velocity means for displacement before and after that time.
Recall that displacement is the signed area under the velocity-time graph, with area above the axis positive and area below the axis negative.

Calculate the large positive triangle from $0$ to $16\text{ s}$ with peak $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$, then find the velocity at $20\text{ s}$ and subtract the small negative triangle from $16\text{ s}$ to $20\text{ s}$.
walkthrough: Displacement from $t = 0$ is the signed area under the velocity-time graph from $0$ to $t = 20\text{ s}$, because area $= v \times t$.
From $0$ to $16\text{ s}$ the graph is a triangle above the axis with base $16\text{ s}$ and height $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Its area is $0.5 \times 16 \times 3 = 24\text{ m}$.

From $16\text{ s}$ to $24\text{ s}$ velocity is negative. Velocity falls uniformly from $0$ at $16\text{ s}$ to $-3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $24\text{ s}$, so at $20\text{ s}$ it is $-1.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The signed area from $16\text{ s}$ to $20\text{ s}$ is a small triangle below the axis with base $4\text{ s}$ and height $-1.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Its area is $0.5 \times 4 \times (-1.5) = -3\text{ m}$.
Total displacement at $t = 20\text{ s}$ is $24 + (-3) = 21\text{ m}$. This is option B.
